title: Depth First Search
html:
Depth First Search is one of the main graph algorithms.

Depth First Search finds the lexicographical first path in the graph from a source vertex uuu to each vertex. Depth First Search will also find the shortest paths in a tree (because there only exists one simple path), but on general graphs this is not the case.

The algorithm works in O(m+n)O(m + n)O(m+n) time where nnn is the number of vertices and mmm is the number of edges.

Description of the algorithm

The idea behind DFS is to go as deep into the graph as possible, and backtrack once you are at a vertex without any unvisited adjacent vertices.

It is very easy to describe / implement the algorithm recursively: We start the search at one vertex. After visiting a vertex, we further perform a DFS for each adjacent vertex that we haven't visited before. This way we visit all vertices that are reachable from the starting vertex.

For more details check out the implementation.

Applications of Depth First Search

  • Find any path in the graph from source vertex uuu to all vertices.

  • Find lexicographical first path in the graph from source uuu to all vertices.

  • Check if a vertex in a tree is an ancestor of some other vertex:

    At the beginning and end of each search call we remember the entry and exit "time" of each vertex. Now you can find the answer for any pair of vertices (i,j)(i, j)(i,j) in O(1)O(1)O(1): vertex iii is an ancestor of vertex jjj if and only if entry[i]<entry[j]\text{entry}[i] < \text{entry}[j]entry[i]<entry[j] and exit[i]>exit[j]\text{exit}[i] > \text{exit}[j]exit[i]>exit[j].

  • Find the lowest common ancestor (LCA) of two vertices.

  • Topological sorting:

    Run a series of depth first searches so as to visit each vertex exactly once in O(n+m)O(n + m)O(n+m) time. The required topological ordering will be the vertices sorted in descending order of exit time.

  • Check whether a given graph is acyclic and find cycles in a graph. (As mentioned below by counting back edges in every connected components).

  • Find strongly connected components in a directed graph:

    First do a topological sorting of the graph. Then transpose the graph and run another series of depth first searches in the order defined by the topological sort. For each DFS call the component created by it is a strongly connected component.

  • Find bridges in an undirected graph:

    First convert the given graph into a directed graph by running a series of depth first searches and making each edge directed as we go through it, in the direction we went. Second, find the strongly connected components in this directed graph. Bridges are the edges whose ends belong to different strongly connected components.

Classification of edges of a graph

We can classify the edges of a graph, GGG, using the entry and exit time of the end nodes uuu and vvv of the edges (u,v)(u,v)(u,v). These classifications are often used for problems like finding bridges and finding articulation points.

We perform a DFS and classify the encountered edges using the following rules:

If vvv is not visited:

  • Tree Edge - If vvv is visited after uuu then edge (u,v)(u,v)(u,v) is called a tree edge. In other words, if vvv is visited for the first time and uuu is currently being visited then (u,v)(u,v)(u,v) is called tree edge. These edges form a DFS tree and hence the name tree edges.

If vvv is visited before uuu:

  • Back edges - If vvv is an ancestor of uuu, then the edge (u,v)(u,v)(u,v) is a back edge. vvv is an ancestor exactly if we already entered vvv, but not exited it yet. Back edges complete a cycle as there is a path from ancestor vvv to descendant uuu (in the recursion of DFS) and an edge from descendant uuu to ancestor vvv (back edge), thus a cycle is formed. Cycles can be detected using back edges.

  • Forward Edges - If vvv is a descendant of uuu, then edge (u,v)(u, v)(u,v) is a forward edge. In other words, if we already visited and exited vvv and entry[u]<entry[v]\text{entry}[u] < \text{entry}[v]entry[u]<entry[v] then the edge (u,v)(u,v)(u,v) forms a forward edge.

  • Cross Edges: if vvv is neither an ancestor or descendant of uuu, then edge (u,v)(u, v)(u,v) is a cross edge. In other words, if we already visited and exited vvv and entry[u]>entry[v]\text{entry}[u] > \text{entry}[v]entry[u]>entry[v] then (u,v)(u,v)(u,v) is a cross edge.

Theorem. Let GGG be an undirected graph. Then, performing a DFS upon GGG will classify every encountered edge as either a tree edge or back edge, i.e., forward and cross edges only exist in directed graphs.

Suppose (u,v)(u,v)(u,v) is an arbitrary edge of GGG and without loss of generality, uuu is visited before vvv, i.e., entry[u]<entry[v]\text{entry}[u] < \text{entry}[v]entry[u]<entry[v]. Because the DFS only processes edges once, there are only two ways in which we can process the edge (u,v)(u,v)(u,v) and thus classify it:

  • The first time we explore the edge (u,v)(u,v)(u,v) is in the direction from uuu to vvv. Because entry[u]<entry[v]\text{entry}[u] < \text{entry}[v]entry[u]<entry[v], the recursive nature of the DFS means that node vvv will be fully explored and thus exited before we can "move back up the call stack" to exit node uuu. Thus, node vvv must be unvisited when the DFS first explores the edge (u,v)(u,v)(u,v) from uuu to vvv because otherwise the search would have explored (u,v)(u,v)(u,v) from vvv to uuu before exiting node vvv, as nodes uuu and vvv are neighbors. Therefore, edge (u,v)(u,v)(u,v) is a tree edge.

  • The first time we explore the edge (u,v)(u,v)(u,v) is in the direction from vvv to uuu. Because we discovered node uuu before discovering node vvv, and we only process edges once, the only way that we could explore the edge (u,v)(u,v)(u,v) in the direction from vvv to uuu is if there's another path from uuu to vvv that does not involve the edge (u,v)(u,v)(u,v), thus making uuu an ancestor of vvv. The edge (u,v)(u,v)(u,v) thus completes a cycle as it is going from the descendant, vvv, to the ancestor, uuu, which we have not exited yet. Therefore, edge (u,v)(u,v)(u,v) is a back edge.

Since there are only two ways to process the edge (u,v)(u,v)(u,v), with the two cases and their resulting classifications outlined above, performing a DFS upon GGG will therefore classify every encountered edge as either a tree edge or back edge, i.e., forward and cross edges only exist in directed graphs. This completes the proof.

Implementation

vector<vector<int>> adj; // graph represented as an adjacency list
int n; // number of vertices

vector<bool> visited;

void dfs(int v) {
	visited[v] = true;
	for (int u : adj[v]) {
		if (!visited[u])
			dfs(u);
    }
}

This is the most simple implementation of Depth First Search. As described in the applications it might be useful to also compute the entry and exit times and vertex color. We will color all vertices with the color 0, if we haven't visited them, with the color 1 if we visited them, and with the color 2, if we already exited the vertex.

Here is a generic implementation that additionally computes those:

vector<vector<int>> adj; // graph represented as an adjacency list
int n; // number of vertices

vector<int> color;

vector<int> time_in, time_out;
int dfs_timer = 0;

void dfs(int v) {
	time_in[v] = dfs_timer++;
	color[v] = 1;
	for (int u : adj[v])
		if (color[u] == 0)
			dfs(u);
	color[v] = 2;
	time_out[v] = dfs_timer++;
}
